# The Idle Death: Diagnosing a Car That Starts Then Cuts Out

A vehicle that cranks, fires up, and immediately stalls is a classic symptom of an engine control unit (ECU) failing to maintain closed-loop operation. In your specific scenario with the 2006 Honda Civic, the fact that dash lights and headlights functioned during the jump start confirms power delivery was sufficient at the battery terminals. However, the immediate shutdown upon starting indicates the engine management system could not sustain idle speed or synchronize fuel injection with airflow.

When you attempted to jump-start the car after three months of inactivity, several chemical and electrical changes likely occurred simultaneously. Lead-acid batteries degrade rapidly when left in a discharged state; even if they appear to hold a charge under load (enough to light up the dashboard), their capacity may be insufficient to drive the high-current demands of the fuel pump and ignition system during the critical seconds after startup. The ECU relies on stable voltage from the alternator once the engine spins, but if the battery cannot bridge the gap between cranking and charging, the system reverts to a "fail-safe" mode or simply dies because the ignition coils lose the necessary voltage to fire.

The most probable culprit here is fuel starvation caused by evaporative emissions system failure, specifically a clogged fuel filter or degraded fuel pump screen. Modern ECUs operate in an open-loop state during startup, ignoring oxygen sensor feedback until the engine warms up. If the fuel pressure drops below the threshold required for injection, the ECU will cut fuel to prevent flooding or runaway conditions, causing the engine to die instantly. This is a common failure mode in vehicles sitting idle for extended periods because gasoline degrades into varnish and gums up the fuel injectors and pump screen over time.

Another critical area to investigate is the ignition switch or the starter solenoid circuit. On many Hondas of this era, the ignition lock cylinder contains contacts that wear out. When you turn the key to the "Run" position after a cold start, the electrical continuity might be momentary. If the ECU loses power for even 50 milliseconds while it is transitioning from cranking to idle, it will reset and cut fuel injectors immediately.

To troubleshoot this systematically without replacing parts blindly, start by checking the battery's Cold Cranking Amps (CCA) rating against your multimeter. A healthy battery should read above 12.6V when fully charged. If you are unable to verify voltage under load, a load tester is essential because a weak battery will mimic an alternator failure. Next, inspect the fuel pump relay location (often found in the fuse box under the hood or near the firewall). You can listen for the distinct whir of the fuel pump priming when you turn the key to "On" before cranking; if there is silence, the pump or its relay has failed.

If the vehicle has no mechanical problems prior to this, the issue is almost certainly electrical degradation exacerbated by the three-month idle. The jump start provided a temporary voltage boost, masking the underlying low state of charge in the battery and the inability of the fuel system to deliver consistent pressure once the alternator wasn't yet charging the system.

If you have access to diagnostic tools, connecting an OBD-II scanner can reveal whether the ECU is logging fuel trim codes (like P0171 or P0174) or ignition misfire codes immediately after startup. These codes would confirm if the engine is starving for air/fuel mixture or losing spark. Without such tools, a systematic replacement of the battery followed by a check of the fuel pump relay and fuse is the most logical first step before assuming catastrophic failure of the ECU itself.
